I’ve been like a storm no one can predict. For the past couple of months, I couldn’t sit still—I was up at 4 a.m. rewriting the entire menu, calling suppliers, launching a catering side business with no plan. I felt electric, like I could run the restaurant, two more, and still have energy to spare. I talked so fast my staff said I was hard to follow. I even flirted aggressively with customers, which isn’t like me… my husband noticed. I spent thousands on glassware and a food truck deposit—just a feeling I *had* to act.  

But then… it crashed. For months now, I can’t get out of bed. I don’t enjoy my daughter’s laughter, I don’t enjoy food—nothing. I stare at my closet for 20 minutes, paralyzed by what to wear. I think… I think my husband is hiding something. I’ve seen him—no, not him, but *shadows* of him—coming out of another room, dressed differently. Other times, I swear I see someone standing at the end of the bar, watching me, but when I look, it’s empty.  

The mood swings—up, down, furious, then numb—have wrecked everything. I don’t know if the voices in my head started during the highs or if they stay after. I can’t tell what’s real anymore, and I don’t know when it began.
D010-D006_h001.question_a:
I’ve been running my restaurant for twelve years, and up until two months ago, everything was steady. But then things started spiraling. I suddenly felt unstoppable—like I could open three more locations overnight. I spent $80,000 renovating a second site without telling my husband, convinced it was a genius move. I barely slept, but I wasn’t tired. My mind raced, and I couldn’t stop talking—my staff said I’d interrupt them mid-sentence, firing off ideas.  

My mood swung wildly—one minute I was laughing about launching a food truck empire, the next I was screaming at my chef over a delayed delivery. I started flirting with customers, even had a moment where I thought about meeting one after hours. That’s not me.  

I also started seeing things—out of the corner of my eye, I’d catch my husband in the kitchen with someone else, but when I turned, no one was there. I became obsessed he was cheating, even though he’s never given me reason.  

This manic spell lasted two months. After it broke, I crashed. For five months, I couldn’t get out of bed. I lost interest in the restaurant, in my husband, in everything. I couldn’t even decide what to wear in the morning. But now I can say the hallucinations and paranoid thoughts only happened during that intense high—never when I was depressed or stable.

And for two weeks last month, my mood was stable—no high, no low—but I still saw shadows and was certain my husband had installed hidden cameras in the house. The voices in my head, the jealousy, the visions—they were still here, even when the mania wasn’t.

I know it sounds off, but I swear sometimes the radio news anchors are sending me coded messages. My wife says it’s stress, but it feels real. I’ve been talking nonstop, even at home. My wife says I jump between topics so fast she can’t follow. I took out a loan to start a “transport business” last week—no plan, no contacts—but it made perfect sense at the time. And I keep hearing voices—just my name, whispered, when no one’s there.

The second I calmed down a bit, they faded. They only ever show up *with* the restless energy and the rage. I’d start five different cases at once, call clients at 3 a.m., jump from one lead to another, couldn’t sit still during stakeouts—just pacing, scribbling notes, feeling like I was onto something huge. I felt unstoppable… then, suddenly, furious if someone questioned me. 

During that time, I started hearing voices—two men arguing behind me, even when no one was there. I knew the police were tracking me, probably working with one of my ex-clients. I could *feel* the cameras everywhere. But once that two-week rush faded, the energy crashed. For the past two months, I haven’t touched my job. Lost interest in everything—cars, surveillance, even boxing, which I used to love. I pace the apartment, wring my hands, can’t stay seated. Sometimes I get this sudden urge to just… run into the street, step off the roof—but I don’t plan it. It just *hits*. 

The voices? They’re gone. Only came during that manic spell.
D010-D006_h024.question_b:
I’ve been feeling… off for the past few months—actually, closer to two and a half months now. It started with this high energy—like I didn’t need sleep, I was calling clients at 3 a.m., tailing people all night, jumping from one case to another without finishing a single one. One minute I’d feel on top of the world, like I could crack any case, then suddenly I’d be furious at some imagined slight from a client or think my phone was tapped. I kept hearing whispers too—clear as day—like two guys in suits talking about me in low voices, even when no one was around. I started believing there was a conspiracy, maybe linked to a case I’d worked last year. I truly thought I was being followed, watched through cameras.

That manic phase lasted about two weeks, but even after it faded—the racing thoughts slowed a bit—I still heard those voices. They never really went away, even when I crashed into this deep funk where I couldn’t care less about cases, couldn’t get off the couch. I’d pace for hours, wringing my hands, and this urge would hit me—suddenly wanting to jump off my apartment roof, not because I wanted to die, but like the urge was just *there*, screaming.

The paranoia and voices stuck around for weeks after the mania was gone—still here some days.

D010-D006_h025.question_both:
I’ve been through some highs and lows lately—more than I can remember having in years. About two weeks straight a few months back, I felt incredible—like I’d tapped into something brilliant. I was writing three books at once, pacing around the house at all hours, barely sleeping. My wife says I couldn’t finish a sentence without jumping to a new idea. I started rewriting old manuscripts, designing covers, even pitching TV adaptations—none of which I ever followed through on.  

Then it all crashed. For two months, I couldn’t get out of my chair. Moving felt like wading through mud. I stopped writing altogether, not because I didn’t care about my work, but because success suddenly seemed meaningless. I kept thinking, “Does any of this matter?” I wouldn’t mind if I didn’t wake up one morning.  

The strange part? I started tasting pennies—even when I wasn’t eating anything. And sometimes, I’d hear neighbors laughing and just *know* they were mocking sentences from my unpublished novels. I can’t say for sure if they were. I haven’t told my wife those parts.  

The timing… I can’t quite place it—whether the voices came only during the high, or lingered after. It’s all blurred.

And I became convinced that small comments people made—like the mailman saying “Have a good one”—were secret messages directed at me, coded praise for my genius. I even tasted metal constantly, though I wasn’t eating anything unusual. But when that burst of energy faded, I crashed. For the last two months, I’ve barely gotten out of bed. Moving feels like wading through mud. I don’t care about the books I left unfinished—used to take pride in my work, but now it all feels meaningless. Once the mania passed, those stopped—only the heaviness remained.
D010-D006_h025.question_b:

I felt completely numb, like my body was made of stone—moving, speaking, even lifting a cup took so much effort. I stopped caring about my writing, which used to be everything to me. I’d think, “What’s the point? None of it matters.” I even hoped I wouldn’t wake up some mornings, though I’d never act on it.

Before that, though, I was completely opposite—full of energy, up for days writing ten different stories, calling publishers at 3 a.m., starting book projects I never finished. I’d jump from one idea to another, convinced each was genius. I believed people on the radio were sending me coded messages about my work—specific compliments meant only I could understand. And sometimes, I’d taste something metallic in my mouth, even if I hadn’t eaten. My wife says it wasn’t real, but I *felt* it.

The key thing is, even when I wasn’t manic or depressed, those voices and tastes stuck around for weeks. And if I’m honest, the manic bursts have taken up most of the last two years.
